issues.explanation: 'Avoid Work or Study: Going to work or study' directly conflicts with 'Overwork: work excessively to avoid being alone with thoughts' within the same maladaptive strategies node. Excessive work engagement and avoidance of work/study are opposing coping patterns and, without any qualifier distinguishing contexts, are clinically contradictory.

vignette: Leilani had always loved the ocean, growing up in a small coastal town where her family made their living from fishing. At 19, she was already an experienced fisherman, but it was on one fateful day out at sea that her life took a dramatic turn. She witnessed a horrific accident involving another boat, and though she wasn't physically harmed, the memory of the screams and chaos has haunted her ever since. The sounds of that day still lingered in her mind - the screeching of metal, the cries for help - and would often trigger vivid flashbacks. But it was more than just auditory triggers; even something as mundane as footsteps behind or nearby could send her heart racing. When she rode her bicycle to work, the rhythmic thud of pedals on pavement might suddenly transport her back to that fateful day. To avoid these unwanted memories, Leilani began working excessively long hours out at sea, hoping the physical exhaustion would numb her mind. She'd also spend hours scrolling through her phone or playing games, anything to distract herself from the thoughts that threatened to overwhelm her. But no matter how hard she tried, the memories still forced their way into her mind unbidden. Sometimes, she'd feel an intense emotional surge without even realizing why - a sudden wave of guilt or anxiety that left her breathless and bewildered. When these episodes occurred, Leilani couldn't shake the feeling that her body was betraying her, reacting as if she were still in danger when logically she knew she was safe. As time went on, Leilani became increasingly convinced that she'd failed to protect others during the accident - a thought that filled her with self-loathing and fear of her own rage. She began avoiding intimacy with her partner, unable to shake the notion that she might lose control and do something terrible. Her mind was constantly on high alert, anticipating threats around every corner - when delays occurred or things didn't go according to plan, Leilani's anxiety spiked, and her body would react before her mind had time to catch up. This self-perpetuating cycle of fear and avoidance only intensified as the months passed. Leilani found herself withdrawing from social interactions, unable to concentrate on even simple tasks, and plagued by a creeping sense of dread that she couldn't shake. Her partner tried to be supportive, but Leilani pushed them away, fearing her own anger and feeling like a ticking time bomb. It was this fear - the terror of losing control and causing harm to those she loved - that finally brought Leilani to seek help. She knew she needed to confront these demons head-on if she wanted any chance at rebuilding her life. As she sat in the therapist's office, her eyes brimming with tears, Leilani whispered a simple yet heartbreaking truth: "I just want to feel safe again."
